Checking compatibility with Vercel and Next.js 16.

Vercel supports Next.js 16.4.0 natively. Environment variables must be configured in the Vercel dashboard. APP_ORIGINS needs the exact production domain and any preview URLs; localhost values will cause token rejection. Camera works over HTTPS. Live video does not stream through Vercel.

No vercel.json is required. Vercel ignores custom start scripts and uses its own serverless runtime after `next build`. The Node runtime route is valid since it is not Edge. The pnpm packageManager field is read by Vercel. Live video streams directly from Decart to the browser. Vercel function timeouts and bandwidth limits do not affect the live stream. OBS browser sources load the public HTTPS /obs page. Subscribe tokens are passed in the URL.

The public deployment warning from the README still applies. The Vercel URL is public unless protected with password or deployment protection. The .env.example file contains a real API key. Do not commit it. Set the environment variables only in the Vercel dashboard.

_**Agent (default)**_

Yes. This can be deployed and used on Vercel. The live video does not run on Vercel.

Vercel only hosts the Next.js UI and the short token API (`/api/realtime-token`). The browser gets a short-lived token, then talks to Decart directly for the camera stream. Camera and the OBS page both work there because Vercel serves the site over HTTPS.

Set these in the Vercel project environment, not in the repo:

- `DECART_API_KEY` — the permanent Decart key
- `APP_ORIGINS` — the exact site origin, for example `https://your-app.vercel.app`

`http://localhost:3000` will not work on the deployed site. The studio will load, but live start stays disabled until that origin matches the URL in the browser. Each Vercel preview URL is different, so a preview only works if that exact origin is in `APP_ORIGINS`. A stable production domain is the practical one to allow.

The public URL can mint billable Decart tokens for anyone who can open it. Turn on Vercel deployment protection, or put it behind your own login, if the site should not be open.

_**User**_

when do i need rtmp and hls ?

---

_**Agent (default)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Determining when RTMP and HLS are needed for this LiveBridge/Decart studio project, which currently uses WebRTC and an OBS browser source.

WebRTC is low-latency and real-time, ideal for interactive camera feeds but hard to scale to thousands of viewers without a media server.

OBS can encode the WebRTC feed for further distribution. RTMP is a push protocol used to send a live stream to a server such as YouTube, Twitch, or Mux. It requires a destination that accepts ingest and typically introduces a few seconds of delay. HLS is a playback protocol.

HLS splits the stream into small HTTP segments and a playlist file. It is ideal for websites, mobile apps, and CDNs serving large audiences. Normal HLS latency is five to thirty seconds, though low-latency variants reach two to five seconds. Use it when viewers need a standard HTTP video URL or when the platform only accepts an HTTP stream. The typical pipeline is Camera → WebRTC → OBS Browser Source → OBS encodes and pushes RTMP to a platform, which then serves viewers via HLS.

No extra protocols are needed for local browser use or OBS recordings. RTMP is required only when pushing to a platform that demands a stream URL and key. HLS is needed only when sharing a watchable URL with a standard video player.
</details></think>

_**Agent (default)**_

You need **RTMP** when a platform asks you to send it a live broadcast. YouTube, Twitch, Facebook, and most restream tools give you an RTMP URL plus a stream key. OBS encodes the picture and pushes that feed to them. This app never does that step.

You need **HLS** when other people should watch in a normal video player. The platform turns the RTMP feed into an `.m3u8` link, and phones, browsers, and CDNs play that link. Latency is usually several seconds.

For this project the path is:

1. **WebRTC** — your camera goes to Decart and back, inside the browser. That is all the app does.
2. **OBS Browser Source** — OBS loads the `/obs` page and shows that WebRTC picture in a scene.
3. **RTMP** — only if you then click Start Streaming in OBS toward YouTube, Twitch, or a similar ingest.
4. **HLS** — only if viewers should watch that broadcast through the platform’s player, not through your studio page.

Stay on WebRTC and the OBS page when you are previewing, recording locally, or putting the transformed camera into an OBS scene. Add RTMP when you go live to a platform. HLS shows up on the viewing side of that platform, not in this repo.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The user wants OBS to capture only the AI screen side rather than the full studio page.

The project already supports this. Copy the OBS link after starting a live session and add it as a Browser Source in OBS. Match the browser source dimensions to the canvas. The video uses object-fit: contain, so black bars may appear if the aspect ratios differ. The "Connecting..." message may flash briefly. The link expires once the session ends.

_**Agent (default)**_

Use the **OBS output** link from the studio. That page is only the AI video, full-screen on a black background. Do not point OBS at the studio page or at a window capture of the whole app.

1. Start the live session in the studio.
2. Under **OBS output**, click **Copy OBS link**. The link appears only while that session is connected.
3. In OBS, add a source: **Browser**.
4. Paste the copied link. Set the width and height to your canvas, for example 1920×1080.
5. Leave **Shutdown source when not visible** off, and check **Refresh browser when scene becomes active** if the picture stays black the first time.

The video is fit inside that rectangle, so a mismatch between the AI frame and your canvas shows as black bars. Match the browser source size to the canvas, then crop in OBS if you still see bars.

That link dies when you stop the session. Start live again and copy a new one.

_**Agent (default)**_

`/ai` in Zamvc is an OBS-only view of the AI video. It lives in the Vite demo at `examples/react-vite`, not in the main Laravel app.

The same React app serves two pages:

- `/` is the control page. You upload a photo, start the call, and see your camera and the AI result side by side.
- `/ai` skips that UI and renders only a full-screen black video of the AI result.

OBS is a separate browser, so it cannot see the camera stream from the main page. When the call connects, the main page posts Decart’s `subscribeToken` to `/api/call-token`. The `/ai` page polls that endpoint every second and joins the same call as a viewer. It does not start a second generation.

In OBS, add a Browser source and open `/ai` (for example `http://localhost:5173/ai`). Leave the main page open. Stopping the call clears the token, and `/ai` goes black.

That token bridge exists only in the Vite dev server. A production build of this example does not include `/api/call-token`.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Comparing the Zamvc `/ai` approach against LiveBridge's existing `/obs` setup to determine if adding `/ai` to the project is the right move.

LiveBridge's `/obs` is output-only and fullscreen. It uses server-side tokens passed in the URL hash. It works on Vercel without in-memory state. Zamvc's `/ai` uses a fixed path.

No. Zamvc's `/ai` relies on a Vite dev server that holds one global token in memory. It does not work in production. LiveBridge's `/obs` is the proper replacement. Adding `/ai` would be a step backward.

Vercel serverless instances cannot share the Vite dev server's in-memory token, so OBS and the studio would hit different instances and lose the stream. Zamvc also places the permanent API key in the client, which would undo this project's security model of issuing short-lived server-side tokens. Adding `/ai` would duplicate the existing `/obs` screen.

A stable URL is the only real UX benefit of `/ai`. LiveBridge's current links already change per session. A proper stable route would still use server-issued tokens instead of copying the Vite in-memory bridge.
</details></think>

_**Agent (default)**_

No. Do not add Zamvc’s `/ai` to this project.

This app already has that page. `/obs` is the AI video only, full screen, for an OBS Browser Source. Zamvc’s `/ai` is the same idea, built for a Vite dev server.

Copying it would be the weaker version here. Zamvc keeps one subscribe token in the dev server’s memory, and the browser holds the permanent Decart key. That works on your machine while `vite` is running. On Vercel, each request can hit a different server, so that stored token disappears, and putting the permanent key in the browser is what this project is built to avoid.

`/obs` already does the proper version: the studio link carries the subscribe token, and the server gives OBS a short-lived key. Set the OBS Browser Source to that link after you start the live session.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The muesli obs-cli cannot create browser sources.

The muesli obs-cli only lists and mutes existing sources. It targets the legacy obs-websocket v4 protocol. Modern OBS 28+ uses the v5 protocol instead. Better alternatives include `obs-cmd`, `obsws-cli`, and `obsws-python`.

OBS 28+ includes obs-websocket natively. The obs64.exe binary has no built-in flag to add a browser source. A CLI wrapper must send the `CreateInput` request over the websocket. This is the standard approach.

Enable the WebSocket server in OBS and set a password on port 4455. The CLI wrapper then calls `GetSceneList` to locate the target scene. It sends a `CreateInput` request with `inputKind: browser_source` and settings including the URL, resolution, and restart flags.

The browser source needs a one-time creation step. The session token inside the URL is generated only after the user starts a live stream. The CLI must therefore call `SetInputSettings` to refresh the URL whenever the token changes.

The muesli obs-cli cannot create or update browser sources. A v5-capable client such as obs-cmd is required. I am checking whether obs-cmd supports raw CreateInput requests or if a small custom script is needed instead.
</details></think>

_**Agent (default)**_

OBS itself cannot add a source from `obs64.exe`. The way to do it from a command line is the WebSocket server that is already built into OBS 28 and later. The usual CLI for that is `obsws-cli`. The older `obs-cli` can switch scenes and start a stream, and it cannot create a Browser source.

The link this app gives you is only valid after you press **Start live**. It looks like `https://your-host/obs#token=...&model=lucy-latest`. The part after `#` changes every session, so the CLI has to update that URL each time. Adding a new source every session would pile up duplicates.

**Once**

1. In OBS, open **Tools → WebSocket Server Settings**, turn the server on, and set a password. The default port is `4455`. Leave OBS running.
2. Install `obsws-cli` and point it at that server (`--host`, `--port`, `--password`).
3. Create one Browser source in the scene you stream from. The input kind is `browser_source`, and a clear name is `LiveBridge`. Set the width and height to the canvas, usually `1920` and `1080`. Leave **Shutdown source when not visible** off, and turn **Refresh browser when scene becomes active** on.

**Every live session**

1. Start this app and press **Start live**.
2. Copy the **OBS output** link. The token in that link is the whole permission to view the AI video.
3. Tell OBS to set that source’s `url` to the copied link. In the WebSocket protocol that request is `SetInputSettings`, with `overlay` left on so the size stays put.
4. When you stop the session, that link dies. Start live again and send the new link to the same source.

OBS and the browser that runs the studio can be on the same PC, and then `http://localhost:3000` is a valid origin. If OBS is on another machine, the link has to be the public HTTPS address, and that exact origin has to be in `APP_ORIGINS`.

---

```
   - Rate limit /obs to stop key guessing.
   - Add your site address to APP_ORIGINS.
```

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
A bug exists in the subscribe logic. activeToken is set before the call, but the function checks activeToken against subscribeToken inside.

The race condition is safe. clearVideo resets activeToken to null before subscribe begins, so the check aborts correctly. tick clears the token before setting it. subscribe does not modify activeToken on entry.

Running type checks. A type issue exists in the publish route model. Assigning a ref during render is valid despite potential React compiler warnings.

clearVideo disconnects the subscriber and nulls the reference. The error handler checks subscriber !== nextSubscriber after this nulling, so it exits safely. However, the disconnect may trigger a re-entry into connectionChange.

Nulling the subscriber reference before calling disconnect prevents recursive re-entry into clearVideo. The error handler will then see a mismatched subscriber and exit safely.

The clearVideo implementation now stores the subscriber locally, nulls the global reference, resets activeToken, and then disconnects. This ordering guarantees the error handler sees a mismatched subscriber and exits safely even if disconnect triggers a synchronous re-entry. The obs-viewer component needs the same update. In subscribe, the new subscriber is assigned only after the await resolves; if clearVideo ran during that window, the activeToken mismatch prevents the new subscriber from being connected.

A 429 response preserves the live video instead of clearing it. The session route imports RealtimeModelName correctly. The startSession catch block invokes stopSession, which clears state. The live-studio component may trigger ESLint warnings from assigning a ref during render, so type checks and linting will be verified.

A race condition exists between an in-flight publishViewer request and stop. If the publish request arrives after clearVideo nulls the session ID, it may overwrite the cleared state and restore the video. The server last-write-wins model cannot detect this out-of-order arrival. A generation counter or a server-side session ID check would prevent stale publishes from overriding the clear.

A tombstone list of recently cleared session IDs is the preferred fix. The server would store the last 20 cleared IDs and ignore late publishes for those sessions. Waiting for the client to finish its publish before stopping is unreliable on unmount.

The server will track retired session IDs in a capped list. A publish for a retired ID is ignored and returns true so the client does not error. This handles both late publishes and late clears safely.

The server will cap the retired session ID list at twenty entries. Each studio instance generates a fresh UUID on start, so a legitimate retry of the same session ID will not be blocked by the tombstone. The obs-state file will include the new `retiredSessionIds` array from creation, and the publish handler will check this list before accepting a token.

The server will always retire a session ID on clear, even if the live state does not match, preventing late publishes from resurrecting the view. Retired IDs will be added to the capped list and duplicates filtered out. The readState helper will default the new array to empty. The viewer component also needs its clearVideo race fixed.

Returning true for retired sessions prevents a false error when the client's publishViewer resolves after the user stops. The mounted check may fail because stop nulls the realtime reference, so the error guard might not catch it anyway. The tombstone list remains the primary fix for the resurrection bug. Now updating obs-state.
</details></think>

```bash
$late = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$origin/api/obs/session" -Method POST -Headers ($headers + @{ "x-obs-publish-secret" = $secret }) -Body (@{ sessionId = $session; subscribeToken = "late-token"; model = "lucy-latest" } | ConvertTo-Json) -SkipHttpErrorCheck

} | ConvertTo-Json
```

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The HTTP status code was concatenated with the response body. The `-o NUL` option likely failed, causing the body to print and corrupting the status code output.

The "403000" output suggests the HTTP status code was concatenated with a trailing "000", possibly from a failed write or a second request. PowerShell does not interpret percent signs inside double quotes, so the curl.exe alias is unlikely to blame.

The 400 error may stem from JSON escaping issues when passing the payload through PowerShell.

The 400 error means the request failed validation before reaching the secret check. Invalid JSON from escaping caused the failure. A temporary JSON file and separate status output should isolate the problem. The inconsistent "400" versus "403000" output remains puzzling.

The `clear` command returned a clean "400" while other requests produced "400000". Complex JSON payloads likely trigger the concatenation bug. I will switch to a temporary file for the body to avoid escaping issues. I will also redirect output to a temp file and add a newline before the status code to isolate the exact curl behavior.

**Regenerate** makes a new link. The old Browser source stops working, so you would paste the new one into OBS.

The link can only watch. It cannot start or replace the live session. The studio publishes that separately, and the publish secret is not shown and is not part of the OBS URL.

The key and the current session are stored in `data/obs-state.json` on this machine. That file is ignored by git. It lasts on a normal server. It will not last on Vercel.

```bash
@'
const url = "http://localhost:3000/obs?key=zam";
const ws = new WebSocket("ws://127.0.0.1:4455");
const pending = new Map();
let requestId = 0;

function request(requestType, requestData = {}) {
  const id = String(++requestId);
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: 6, d: { requestType, requestId: id, requestData } }));
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => pending.set(id, { resolve, reject }));
}

ws.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  const message = JSON.parse(event.data);
  if (message.op === 0) {
    if (message.d.authentication) {
      console.error("obs-auth-required");
      ws.close();
      process.exit(2);
    }
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ op: 1, d: { rpcVersion: 1 } }));
    return;
  }
  if (message.op === 2) {
    void setup();
    return;
  }
  if (message.op === 7) {
    const waiter = pending.get(message.d.requestId);
    if (!waiter) return;
    pending.delete(message.d.requestId);
    if (message.d.requestStatus.result) waiter.resolve(message.d.responseData);
    else waiter.reject(new Error(message.d.requestStatus.comment || "OBS request failed"));
  }
});

async function setup() {
  const scene = await request("GetCurrentProgramScene");
  const inputs = await request("GetInputList");
  const existing = (inputs.inputs || []).some((input) => input.inputName === "LiveBridge");
  const settings = { url, width: 1920, height: 1080, shutdown: false, restart_when_active: true };
  if (existing) {
    await request("SetInputSettings", { inputName: "LiveBridge", inputSettings: settings, overlay: true });
  } else {
    await request("CreateInput", {
      sceneName: scene.sceneName,
      inputName: "LiveBridge",
      inputKind: "browser_source",
      inputSettings: settings,
      sceneItemEnabled: true,
    });
  }
  const saved = await request("GetInputSettings", { inputName: "LiveBridge" });
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    scene: scene.sceneName,
    action: existing ? "updated" : "created",
    url: saved.inputSettings.url,
    width: saved.inputSettings.width,
    height: saved.inputSettings.height,
  }));
  ws.close();
}

ws.addEventListener("error", () => {
  console.error("websocket-failed");
  process.exit(1);
});
```

_**User**_

The issue with your current layout is in your CSS media query:

```css
@media (min-width: 860px) {
  .video-pair { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 16px; }
}

```

When the screen is wider than 860px, `.video-pair` switches from stacked (`grid-template-columns: 1fr`) to side-by-side (`1fr 1fr`). Because your main layout `.studio-layout` reserves 300px to 360px for the sidebar on the right, the main column runs out of horizontal width. As a result, the two videos squish down to ~214px wide while maintaining their `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9`, which forces them to become tiny.

To fix this so your videos stay large (roughly ~460px wide) side-by-side, you need to either give the main content area more breathing room by moving the breakpoint up or letting the layout stack until the screen is wide enough to support two full-sized 16:9 feeds.

Here are the exact fixes to apply to your CSS:

Here is the updated portion of your CSS to replace those two rules:

```css
@media (min-width: 1100px) {
  .video-pair { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 16px; }
}

@media (max-width: 1199px) {
  .studio-layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}

```

To keep your camera preview and AI output side-by-side across tablet, desktop, and mobile screens without letting them stack vertically, you need to remove the mobile media queries that force single-column layout and use a fixed horizontal flex container or CSS grid with a minimum width constraint.

Here is how to modify your CSS so the two video elements remain side-by-side permanently:

Here is the exact snippet of your CSS to update:

```css
/* Force the video pair to always stay side-by-side */
.video-pair { 
  display: grid; 
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; 
  gap: 12px; 
}

/* Ensure the main layout keeps its side-by-side sidebar structure across all screen sizes */
.studio-layout { 
  display: grid; 
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(280px, 340px); 
  gap: 18px; 
  align-items: start; 
}

```

_**Agent (default)**_

The camera and the AI output now stay side by side on every screen size. The rules that stacked them, and the rule that dropped the sidebar into a single column, are gone.

The sidebar stays beside the controls as well. Its column is `minmax(280px, 340px)`. The other column uses a 220px minimum instead of 0, so the mode controls cannot collapse away on a phone.

On a desktop window the two feeds are about 572×321. On a tablet they are about 330×186. On a phone they remain next to each other, about 236×133, because that screen is only 390px wide.
